body:
You are drafting DIALOGUE LINES for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in the exact format asked. No commentary.

## The game
"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player turn-based tactical party RPG (fully voiced, branching dialogue, skill checks, a storyteller Narrator). Folk-horror campaign set in Druskenvald, an afterlife realm of endless night under a gargantuan crescent moon with a leering crone's face. Drawn like a 1960s monster cartoon stuck in Halloween, but the story is real folk horror: stakes, doomed innocents, sacrifice. Humour is deadpan and sits inside the dread. Everything is our own invention in our own words.

## This chapter: Maidenmist Cemetery
South-east of the village of Wickermoor, an endless fogbound cemetery fenced with cold iron is really a prison built over a tear into the Shroud, the mist of death that rings the realm. Wrathful soul-stripped spirits called the shrouded would pour out of it. Its sexton is YORGRIM, the ghost of an orc seer of the Shadestone Clan, who was tricked by his chieftain into a ritual that annihilated his whole clan's souls; he drags a gravestone carved with their names chained to his back as penance. He is dour, stoic, few words, never cruel, tells what matters, and grows vaguer and more distracted as the chapter goes; deep slow orc bass, short flat sentences, long pauses. His spectral black hound ISOLDE (white eyes, a hooded lantern in her mouth) does not speak: only the Narrator describes her. He asked five friends to kindle balefire beacons from fragments of their souls: Sir Marius Renathyr (knight of a morning god, horse Dawn, King Viktor Denathria), Lethica Nightborne (priestess of the Nightmother, barn owl, loved Marius), Ol' Jericho Sticks (kindly scarecrow banjo man), Captain Briggsy Kratch (pirate with a heart of gold, lucky, a swordsman and schemer), Farryn of the Greenwood (satyr druid of the Green Queen, loved Gwenna). They fell to the Horned King's sin and the heroes (the player's party of four, level nine) killed them. The beacons went dark, the tear grew, the dead walked into Wickermoor. The heroes relight the beacons with Final Rites that honour who the Fallen were before they fell, then go below, where Yorgrim breaks and becomes the Chained Reaper; they destroy him and perform his own rites to seal the tear.
Wickermoor people: MORI SHADE, undertaker, grave, stately, white hair, all black, a fount of folklore, follows the Strangers' ways learned from Yorgrim; DORIS SQUIRE, constable, tall, stocky, says the fewest words possible, flat northern burr; TOBIAS DIBBS, Mori's apprentice, relentlessly cheerful and practical; HESTER BOLTON, annoyed her husband Gregor is now a ghast and still owes rent; ADELA DRUSKENVALD (transatlantic 1920s patter); WESTON MURDOCH (warm revival preacher); Theodora Mayville the postmaster is secretly a pigeon hag.

## The Narrator
The Narrator is the Vagrant, a frog-faced ferryman telling the tale afterwards: warm, folksy, wry, fond of the party; never gloats. Second person, present tense, only what a hero could perceive, concrete senses (smell, sound, texture), no game words (HP, roll, level, check, DC, save), no modern slang, never "suddenly". Never name a specific hero (the party is addressed as "you" or "the party").

## Format rules
- One line of plain text per key, written as `key: text`. No quotes around the text, no stage directions, no asterisks, no emoji, no em dashes (use commas, periods, colons), straight quotes only, no brackets.
- A spoken line is one to three short sentences, 12 to 38 words, never over 45. Narrator lines are one or two sentences, never over 45 words. People speak plainly in their own voice; they do not explain the plot to the audience.
- Obey each brief's sentence count and content. Every line must carry a concrete detail.
- Do not put speaker names at the start of the text. Do not repeat the brief.


## Lines to draft (key | speaker | mood | brief). Reply with one `key: text` line for each key and nothing else.

post_lane | Narrator | - | The funeral lane needs someone who is not afraid of the dead. One sentence.
post_lane_right | Narrator | - | Siv steps over the corpses as if they were Tuesday, and the lane stands. One sentence.
post_lane_wrong | Narrator | - | The lane breaks and the militia falls back to the square. One sentence.
militia_done | doris_squire | neutral | Doris surveys the four posts and gives her verdict in as few words as possible. Two short sentences.
militia_quit | doris_squire | weary | Doris says she will do it herself, and the village will notice who did not help. Two short sentences.
mori_scene | Narrator | - | Mori Shade stands in the funeral home in her black, white hair loose, a ledger open on the counter. One sentence.
mori_request | mori_shade | sad | Mori Shade, grave and stately: the freshest of the ghasts was Gregor Bolton, whom she took to the cemetery just before the party came. She has not heard from Yorgrim or seen Isolde since. Three sentences.
mori_request2 | mori_shade | weary | Mori: a week ago she found the gates chained, the fog thick, no beacon fires, no lantern. She asks the party to go. Two sentences.
mori_about | mori_shade | neutral | Mori says Maidenmist is a prison over a tear in the mist of death, and that Yorgrim is its sexton. Two sentences.
mori_yorgrim | mori_shade | smile | Mori says Yorgrim is an old orc ghost who taught her her faith; he drags a stone on his back. Two sentences.
mori_accept | mori_shade | neutral | Mori gives the party grave salt for their blades and says to hold iron against the mist; she will burn the dead outside town. Three short sentences.
mori_salt | mori_shade | neutral | Mori hands over another pouch of grave salt, says it is all she can spare. Two short sentences.
mori_return | mori_shade | sad | Mori, stately, grieves Yorgrim in her stoic way, and says the cemetery needs a caretaker; maybe herself. Three sentences.
mori_isolde | mori_shade | smile | Mori says Isolde has been her messenger before and will wait for the next sexton. Two sentences.
dibbs_scene | Narrator | - | In the funeral home a cheerful lad in an apron sharpens a spade as if for a picnic. One sentence.
dibbs_hello | tobias_dibbs | smile | Tobias Dibbs, Mori's apprentice, relentlessly cheerful and practical: he is delighted to meet people with a good use for a spade. Two sentences.
dibbs_job | tobias_dibbs | neutral | Tobias explains with horrifying practicality what a gravedigger's apprentice does all day. Two sentences.
dibbs_contest | tobias_dibbs | smile | Tobias has collected the dead's own epitaphs; they are too honest; he needs someone to judge a winner, over in the Cremation Gardens. Three short sentences.
epitaph_a | Narrator | - | A brick plaque reads an epitaph the dead wrote for themselves; it is blunt and funny. One sentence.
epitaph_b | Narrator | - | A plaque with an epitaph that complains about the neighbours. One sentence.
epitaph_c | Narrator | - | A plaque with an epitaph that is a very honest confession. One sentence.
epitaph_judge | Narrator | - | Tobias waits by the fountain with a ribbon and a pencil, ready for a verdict. One sentence.
epitaph_win_a | tobias_dibbs | smile | Tobias delighted: the blunt one wins; he pins the ribbon and the dead rustle approval. Two short sentences.
epitaph_win_b | tobias_dibbs | smile | Tobias delighted: the neighbour one wins; the neighbours, he notes, will be furious. Two short sentences.
epitaph_win_c | tobias_dibbs | smile | Tobias delighted: the confession wins; he promises to have it carved before anyone can reconsider. Two short sentences.
epitaph_tie | tobias_dibbs | neutral | Tobias accepts a tie with the air of a man writing three more plaques. Two short sentences.
epitaph_off | tobias_dibbs | sad | Tobias folds his ribbon and says the dead will take it personally; by morning the plaques have scraped their own words off. Two short sentences.
hester_scene | Narrator | - | Hester Bolton stands in the square with her arms folded and her chin up. One sentence.
hester_1 | hester_bolton | angry | Hester Bolton, annoyed: her husband Gregor is now a ghast, and he still owes the landlord rent. Two sentences.
hester_loss | hester_bolton | weary | Hester says her loss is the rent; the husband she can forgive. Two short sentences.
hester_rent | hester_bolton | smile | Hester takes the coins with the dignity of a woman collecting a debt and tells Gregor will hear of it. Two short sentences.
hester_where | hester_bolton | neutral | Hester says Gregor is wherever the ghasts are, and the Mayor's roof is to blame. Two short sentences.
grammar_stone | Narrator | - | At the gate stands a headstone in a prissy hand: HERE LYES A PEDANT, WHO CORRECTS YOU. One or two sentences.
grammar_read | Narrator | - | The headstone clears its throat and corrects the party's pronunciation. One sentence.
result:
post_lane: The muddy funeral lane reeks of grave-rot and needs a steady soul who does not flinch when corpses start to twitch.
post_lane_right: You step over the cold, twitching bodies as if they were Tuesday, and the lantern-lit funeral lane holds fast.
post_lane_wrong: The wooden barricades splinter under dead hands, and the pale militia scrambles back toward the cobbles of the square.
militia_done: Four posts stood, four posts held. That will do until the kettle boils.
militia_quit: Fine, I will haul the pikes and bar the gates myself. Folk round here have long memories for idle hands.
mori_scene: Mori Shade stands in the cedar-scented parlour in her mourning black, her white hair loose above an open leather ledger.
mori_request: The freshest ghast at the barricade was Gregor Bolton, still in his burial linen. I carted his pine coffin to Maidenmist just before you arrived. Neither Yorgrim nor his hound Isolde met me at the gate.
mori_request2: Seven nights ago I found the iron gates chained shut, the fog thick as tallow, and every beacon cold. Walk the hill for me and see why the dead are rising.
mori_about: Maidenmist is no mere boneyard, but an iron prison built over a weeping tear in the Shroud. Old Yorgrim keeps the keys and watches the graves so the rest of us may sleep.
mori_yorgrim: Yorgrim is an old orc spirit who taught me the quiet prayers of the Strangers. He drags a granite headstone chained to his shoulders and never complains of the weight.
mori_accept: Rub this coarse grave salt along your blades before you cross the stile. Keep cold iron between your ribs and the creeping mist. I will stack the fallen out past the ditch and burn them clean.
mori_salt: Take this last linen pouch of consecrated salt from the cellar jar. It is all I can spare before the ash barrels run dry.
mori_return: So the heavy chains are finally off his grey shoulders. Maidenmist still needs a quiet hand to trim the wicks and turn the earth. Perhaps it is time I hung my ledger on the iron gate.
mori_isolde: Isolde has carried her dark lantern to my back door many a frostbitten night. She will curl by the lichgate until the next sexton takes up the spade.
dibbs_scene: Behind the parlour counter, a rosy-cheeked lad in a canvas apron whets an iron spade with a stone as briskly as if packing for a summer picnic.
dibbs_hello: Tobias Dibbs at your service, apprentice in earth and ash. It is a rare treat to meet travellers who know the business end of a good shovel.
dibbs_job: Mostly I drain the bloat, wire the jaws shut so they look polite, and sweep the teeth out of the grate. You work up a grand appetite for mutton pie by noon.
dibbs_contest: The folk here write their own epitaphs before they stiffen, and most are far too honest for church. I propped the best three on the bricks in the Cremation Gardens. Go pick me a champion.
epitaph_a: Scratched into a soot-stained brick is a neat, blunt rhyme: I TOLD THE APOTHECARY THOSE MUSHROOMS WERE SPOTTED, NOW HE IS PAID AND I AM ROTTED.
epitaph_b: A crooked slate plaque beside a clump of nettles reads: BURY ME FACE DOWN SO BARNABY NEXT DOOR CAN KISS WHAT IS LEFT.
epitaph_c: Chiseled deep into a cracked sandstone slab is a belated confession: THE SILVERGRAVE FAMILY SPOONS ARE UNDER THE THIRD FLOORBOARD BY THE CHIMNEY, SORRY MOTHER.
epitaph_judge: Tobias bounces on his heels by the dry stone fountain, twirling a faded blue prize ribbon and a stub of carpenter's pencil.
epitaph_win_a: The mushroom man takes the blue ribbon, short and sweet as arsenic. Listen to the ashes rustling in the urns, they always love a punchline.
epitaph_win_b: A prize for neighbourly spite, and well earned too. Old Barnaby in plot four is going to rattle his lid off when he hears.
epitaph_win_c: Nothing warms the Cremation Gardens like a deathbed confession about stolen silver. I will chisel that in deep before his mother digs herself up to check.
epitaph_tie: A three-way split means nobody sulks and everybody gets a snippet of ribbon. Best fetch my chisel and three fresh bricks from the shed.
epitaph_off: Well, I will fold the ribbon away, though the urns take a snub terribly hard. By cockcrow you will find they have scraped their own letters right off the brick.
hester_scene: Hester Bolton plants her boots on the wet cobbles of the square, her raw red forearms folded tight beneath a lifted chin.
hester_1: My useless husband Gregor has gone and turned himself into a flesh-eating ghast, and the first of the month is tomorrow. Dying twice does not excuse a man from owing six crowns to the landlord.
hester_loss: The man himself I can forgive, he was cold in the feet anyway. It is the six silver crowns for the cellar roof that breaks my heart.
hester_rent: Six honest crowns, warm in the palm and counted twice. When I see Gregor shuffling by the fence, I will tell him a stranger had better manners.
hester_where: Look for Gregor wherever the ghasts are thickest and doing the least work. If the Mayor had mended our leaky slate roof, the damp would never have taken him.
grammar_stone: Beside the rusted iron gate leans a narrow granite headstone engraved in a fussy, pinched hand: HERE LYES A PEDANT, WHO CORRECTS YOU. Below the moss, someone has scratched a comma out and carved it back in deeper.
grammar_read: A dry, papery cough rises from the lichen on the granite slab, and a disembodied voice informs you that lyes is archaic, not an error, and that your vowels are slovenly.
